claim: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells into biofluids such as plasma.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells into biofluids such as plasma.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about EVs.

claim: The separation of EVs from highly abundant free proteins and similarly sized lipoproteins remains technically challenging.
source: The separation of EVs from highly abundant free proteins and similarly sized lipoproteins remains technically challenging.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field about the difficulty of EV isolation.

claim: A digital ELISA assay based on Single Molecule Array (Simoa) technology for ApoB-100 was developed.
source: We developed a digital ELISA assay based on Single Molecule Array (Simoa) technology for ApoB-100, the protein component of several lipoproteins.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and validation of this assay with experimental data.

claim: ApoB-100 is the protein component of several lipoproteins.
source: We developed a digital ELISA assay based on Single Molecule Array (Simoa) technology for ApoB-100, the protein component of several lipoproteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ApoB-100.

claim: Simoa assays for albumin and three tetraspanin proteins found on EVs (CD9, CD63, CD81) were previously developed.
source: Combining this ApoB-100 assay with previously developed Simoa assays for albumin and three tetraspanin proteins found on EVs (Ter-Ovanesyan, Norman et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement cites previous work by the authors.

claim: The five assays (ApoB-100, albumin, CD9, CD63, CD81) enable measurement of the separation of EVs from both lipoproteins and free proteins.
source: Combining this ApoB-100 assay with previously developed Simoa assays for albumin and three tetraspanin proteins found on EVs (Ter-Ovanesyan, Norman et al., 2021), we were able to measure the separation of EVs from both lipoproteins and free proteins.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates this capability through experimental data comparing different isolation methods.

claim: Size exclusion chromatography with resins containing different pore sizes was used to compare EV separation from lipoproteins.
source: We used these five assays to compare EV separation from lipoproteins using size exclusion chromatography with resins containing different pore sizes.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing Sepharose CL-2B, CL-4B, and CL-6B resins.

claim: Improved methods for EV isolation were developed based on combining several types of chromatography resins in the same column.
source: We also developed improved methods for EV isolation based on combining several types of chromatography resins in the same column.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of DMC and TMC columns with experimental validation.

claim: EVs contain RNA and protein cargo from their cell of origin.
source: EVs contain RNA and protein cargo from their cell of origin and are a promising class of biomarkers in biofluids such as plasma (Shah et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2018.

claim: EVs are a promising class of biomarkers in biofluids such as plasma.
source: EVs contain RNA and protein cargo from their cell of origin and are a promising class of biomarkers in biofluids such as plasma (Shah et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2018.

claim: EVs are much less abundant than free proteins and lipoproteins in plasma.
source: Since EVs are much less abundant than free proteins and lipoproteins in plasma, enriching them without the co-isolation of these impurities remains highly challenging (Sódar et al., 2016; Smolarz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sódar et al., 2016 and Smolarz et al., 2019.

claim: Enriching EVs without the co-isolation of free proteins and lipoproteins remains highly challenging.
source: Since EVs are much less abundant than free proteins and lipoproteins in plasma, enriching them without the co-isolation of these impurities remains highly challenging (Sódar et al., 2016; Smolarz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sódar et al., 2016 and Smolarz et al., 2019.

claim: EVs and lipoproteins have overlapping size ranges.
source: This is particularly the case for separating EVs and lipoproteins, as these two classes of particles have overlapping size ranges (Simonsen, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Simonsen, 2017.

claim: Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA) cannot differentiate between EVs and similarly sized lipoproteins.
source: Developing EV isolation methods is also particularly challenging due to the inability of most methods, such as the commonly used Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA) to differentiate between EVs and similarly sized lipoproteins (Johnsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johnsen et al., 2019.

claim: It is difficult to compare EV isolation methods without suitable techniques to quantify both EV yield and lipoprotein content.
source: Thus, it is difficult to compare EV isolation methods without suitable techniques to quantify both EV yield and lipoprotein content (Hartjes et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hartjes et al., 2019.

claim: A framework for comparing EV isolation methods by measuring three tetraspanin transmembrane proteins (CD9, CD63, and CD81) and albumin was previously developed.
source: We have previously developed a framework for comparing EV isolation methods by measuring three tetraspanin transmembrane proteins present on EVs (CD9, CD63, and CD81) and albumin (Ter-Ovanesyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement cites previous work by the authors.

claim: Tetraspanins were used as a way to compare EV yields across different isolation methods.
source: We used the tetraspanins as a way to compare EV yields across different isolation methods and albumin (the most abundant free protein in plasma) as a way to measure protein contamination.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using tetraspanins in the methodology.

claim: Albumin is the most abundant free protein in plasma.
source: We used the tetraspanins as a way to compare EV yields across different isolation methods and albumin (the most abundant free protein in plasma) as a way to measure protein contamination.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about albumin.

claim: Albumin was used as a way to measure protein contamination in EV isolation.
source: We used the tetraspanins as a way to compare EV yields across different isolation methods and albumin (the most abundant free protein in plasma) as a way to measure protein contamination.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using albumin in the methodology.

claim: Single Molecule Array (Simoa) technology is a digital ELISA method that results in high sensitivity and a wide dynamic range.
source: To measure these proteins, we used Single Molecule Array (Simoa) technology, a digital ELISA method that results in high sensitivity and a wide dynamic range (Rissin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rissin et al., 2010.

claim: ApoB-100 is present on low-density lipoproteins (LDL), intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL).
source: ApoB-100 is present on low-density lipoproteins (LDL), intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) (German et al., 2006; Sniderman et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to German et al., 2006 and Sniderman et al., 2019.

claim: Combining the ApoB-100 assay with CD9, CD63, CD81, and albumin assays enables quantification of EVs, lipoproteins, and free proteins for each sample on the same platform.
source: By combining the new ApoB-100 assay with our previously developed CD9, CD63, CD81, and albumin assays, we could quantify EVs, lipoproteins, and free proteins for each sample on the same platform.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates this capability through experimental data.

claim: The developed assays were used to further improve EV isolation methods from plasma.
source: We then used these assays to further improve EV isolation methods from plasma, enabling us to separate EVs from lipoproteins and free proteins at purity levels beyond those of previously described methods.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing improved purity with TMC columns.

claim: The developed methods enable separation of EVs from lipoproteins and free proteins at purity levels beyond those of previously described methods.
source: We then used these assays to further improve EV isolation methods from plasma, enabling us to separate EVs from lipoproteins and free proteins at purity levels beyond those of previously described methods.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing SEC, DMC, and TMC methods.

claim: The developed methods will enable applications requiring high EV purity, such as EV proteomics for biomarker discovery from human biofluids.
source: We envision these methods to enable applications requiring high EV purity, such as EV proteomics for biomarker discovery from human biofluids.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the methods.

claim: Simoa is a digital ELISA method where individual immuno-complexes are trapped on magnetic beads that are loaded into microwells that fit, at most, one bead per well.
source: Simoa is a digital ELISA method where individual immuno-complexes are trapped on magnetic beads that are loaded into microwells that fit, at most, one bead per well.
evidence: This describes the technical principle of Simoa technology.

claim: Counting the 'on wells' in Simoa translates to counting individual protein molecules, providing much higher sensitivity than traditional ELISA.
source: Counting the 'on wells' thus translates to counting individual protein molecules, providing much higher sensitivity than traditional ELISA (Rissin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rissin et al., 2010.

claim: A variety of capture and detector antibodies were compared using calibration curves of the purified ApoB-100 protein standard.
source: First, we compared a variety of capture and detector antibodies using calibration curves of the purified ApoB-100 protein standard.
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure performed in the study.

claim: The antibody pair with the highest signal-to-background ratio was chosen for the ApoB-100 assay.
source: We then chose the antibody pair with the highest signal-to-background ratio (Figure 1A) and validated this assay with dilution linearity experiments in three individual plasma samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria and validation of the assay, supported by Figure 1.

claim: The ApoB-100 assay was validated with dilution linearity experiments in three individual plasma samples.
source: We then chose the antibody pair with the highest signal-to-background ratio (Figure 1A) and validated this assay with dilution linearity experiments in three individual plasma samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes validation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spike and recovery experiments using a purified protein standard were performed for the ApoB-100 assay.
source: We also performed spike and recovery experiments using a purified protein standard (Table 1).
evidence: This describes validation experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The average recovery of 5 ng/ml ApoB-100 spike in plasma was 94.7%.
source: Spike 1	5	94.7
evidence: This value is shown in Table 1.

claim: The average recovery of 10 ng/ml ApoB-100 spike in plasma was 87.2%.
source: Spike 2	10	87.2
evidence: This value is shown in Table 1.

claim: The average recovery of 50 ng/ml ApoB-100 spike in plasma was 90.8%.
source: Spike 3	50	90.8
evidence: This value is shown in Table 1.

claim: The average recovery of 500 ng/ml ApoB-100 spike in plasma was 90.6%.
evidence: This value is shown in Table 1.

claim: EV separation from ApoB-100-containing lipoproteins was investigated using size exclusion chromatography (SEC) columns with three different resins (Sepharose CL-2B, CL-4B, and CL-6B).
source: We tested EV separation based on size using size exclusion chromatography (SEC) columns with three different resins (Sepharose CL-2B, CL-4B, and CL-6B).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 2.

claim: 0.5 ml fractions were collected after performing SEC.
source: We collected 0.5 ml fractions after performing SEC and used Simoa to measure CD9, CD63, CD81, albumin, and ApoB-100 in each fraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Simoa was used to measure CD9, CD63, CD81, albumin, and ApoB-100 in each SEC fraction.
source: We collected 0.5 ml fractions after performing SEC and used Simoa to measure CD9, CD63, CD81, albumin, and ApoB-100 in each fraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Relative EV yields between different EV isolation methods were calculated.
source: As in our previous work (Ter-Ovanesyan et al., 2021), we calculated relative EV yields between different EV isolation methods (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the calculation method with results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EV yield was calculated by determining the ratio of each tetraspanin between conditions and then taking the average of the three tetraspanin ratios.
source: To calculate EV yield, we first determined the ratio of each tetraspanin between conditions and then took the average of the three tetraspanin ratios.
evidence: This describes the calculation methodology.

claim: EV purity was calculated by dividing EV yield by albumin or ApoB-100 levels.
source: To then calculate EV purity, we calculated the ratio of EV yield relative to albumin or ApoB-100 levels.
evidence: This describes the calculation methodology.

claim: The ratio of EVs relative to ApoB-100 was higher in Sepharose CL-2B (the resin with the largest pore size) compared to the other two resins.
source: We found that although the ratio of EVs relative to ApoB-100 was higher in the resin with the largest pore size, Sepharose CL-2B, this was at the expense of EV yield relative to the other two resins (Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The higher ratio of EVs to ApoB-100 in Sepharose CL-2B was at the expense of EV yield relative to the other two resins.
source: We found that although the ratio of EVs relative to ApoB-100 was higher in the resin with the largest pore size, Sepharose CL-2B, this was at the expense of EV yield relative to the other two resins (Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Separating EVs from lipoproteins based on size alone was not fruitful.
source: Because separating EVs from lipoproteins based on size alone was not fruitful, we attempted to separate EVs from lipoproteins based on other properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SEC experiments with different pore sizes.

claim: The separation of EVs from lipoproteins and albumin using density gradient ultracentrifugation (DGC) was investigated.
source: We first investigated the separation of EVs from lipoproteins and albumin using density gradient ultracentrifugation (DGC).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 3.

claim: 1 ml of plasma was loaded on an iodixanol gradient and ultracentrifugation was performed for 16 hr.
source: We loaded 1 ml of plasma on an iodixanol gradient and performed ultracentrifugation for 16 hr.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: 1 ml fractions were collected after density gradient ultracentrifugation.
source: We then collected 1 ml fractions and used Simoa to measure tetraspanins, albumin, and ApoB-100 in each fraction.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: EVs can be readily separated from ApoB-100-containing lipoproteins using density gradient centrifugation.
source: We found that we could readily separate EVs from ApoB-100-containing lipoproteins (Figure 3) using DGC, although the EV yield was lower than in SEC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The EV yield from density gradient centrifugation was lower than in SEC.
source: We found that we could readily separate EVs from ApoB-100-containing lipoproteins (Figure 3) using DGC, although the EV yield was lower than in SEC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DGC is time-consuming and low throughput.
source: As DGC is time-consuming and low throughput, we explored other EV isolation methods that would be more suitable for processing clinical samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of DGC.

claim: The absolute recovery of EVs by SEC using Sepharose CL-6B was assessed.
source: First, we wanted to assess the absolute recovery of EVs by SEC using Sepharose CL-6B, the resin with the highest EV yield (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Simoa's wide dynamic range and specificity were used to measure tetraspanin levels in diluted plasma and compare these levels after EV purification by SEC.
source: We took advantage of Simoa's wide dynamic range and specificity to measure tetraspanin levels in diluted plasma and compared these levels after EV purification from the same batch of plasma by SEC.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Performing at least one 10 ml PBS wash in-column increased the EV yield significantly compared to simply washing the resin in bulk before making the column.
source: We found that performing at least one 10 ml phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) wash in-column, instead of simply washing the resin in bulk before making the column, increased the EV yield significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In-column washes are more effective at removing the ethanol in which the resin is supplied.
source: One potential reason for this result could be that in-column washes are more effective at removing the ethanol in which the resin is supplied.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed result.

claim: Greater than 50% EV yield was achieved using SEC with Sepharose CL-6B after performing an in-column wash.
source: After performing an in-column wash, we were able to achieve >50% EV yield using SEC with Sepharose CL-6B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), as measured by comparing tetraspanin levels in SEC fractions 7–10 relative to diluted plasma.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ApoB-100 is positively charged.
source: We then decided to take advantage of the property that ApoB-100 is positively charged (Olsson et al., 1991), while EVs are generally negatively charged (Brownlee et al., 2014) to separate EVs from lipoproteins.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Olsson et al., 1991.

claim: EVs are generally negatively charged.
source: We then decided to take advantage of the property that ApoB-100 is positively charged (Olsson et al., 1991), while EVs are generally negatively charged (Brownlee et al., 2014) to separate EVs from lipoproteins.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brownlee et al., 2014.

claim: Dual-mode chromatography (DMC) columns with a bottom layer of cation exchange resin below Sepharose CL-4B can be used to isolate EVs.
source: It has previously been demonstrated that dual-mode chromatography (DMC) columns with a bottom layer of cation exchange resin below Sepharose CL-4B can be used to isolate EVs (Van Deun et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Van Deun et al., 2020.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B yields more EVs than Sepharose CL-4B.
source: Since Sepharose CL-6B yields more EVs than Sepharose CL-4B (Figure 2C), we constructed DMC columns with a 2-ml cation exchange resin bottom layer and a top layer of 10 ml Sepharose CL-6B.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DMC columns were constructed with a 2-ml cation exchange resin bottom layer and a top layer of 10 ml Sepharose CL-6B.
source: Since Sepharose CL-6B yields more EVs than Sepharose CL-4B (Figure 2C), we constructed DMC columns with a 2-ml cation exchange resin bottom layer and a top layer of 10 ml Sepharose CL-6B.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A new type of column called Tri-Mode mixed-mode Chromatography (TMC) was developed.
source: Inspired by the DMC approach of combining different resins in the same column, we also developed a new type of column, Tri-Mode mixed-mode Chromatography (TMC), where we further added Capto Core 700 to the cation exchange resin in the bottom layer.
evidence: This describes the development of a new method.

claim: Capto Core 700 is a multimodal chromatography resin that contains porous beads with an inner core layer functionalized with octylamine groups that bind and trap proteins.
source: Capto Core 700 is a multimodal chromatography resin that contains porous beads with an inner core layer functionalized with octylamine groups that bind and trap proteins (Blom et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Blom et al., 2014.

claim: Having Capto Core 700 resin in the bottom layer would 'catch' free proteins that co-isolate with EVs during SEC.
source: Thus, we reasoned that having this resin in the bottom layer would 'catch' free proteins that co-isolate with EVs during SEC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a reasoning about the expected function of the resin.

claim: By changing the volumes and ratios of the two resins in TMC, the depletion of both albumin and ApoB-100 could be tuned to increase purity, although at the cost of EV yield.
source: By changing the volumes and ratios of the two resins, the depletion of both albumin and ApoB-100 could be tuned to increase purity, although at the cost of EV yield (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 2:1 ratio of solid cation exchange resin to multimodal resin in the 2 ml bottom layer was chosen to balance EV yield and purity.
source: To balance EV yield and purity, we settled on a 2:1 ratio of solid cation exchange resin to multimodal resin in the 2 ml bottom layer.
evidence: This describes the optimization of the method.

claim: Electron microscopy was used to image EVs from SEC, DMC, and TMC columns.
source: We first used electron microscopy to image EVs from each column.
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Although lipoproteins were still present, DMC and TMC led to a higher purity of EVs relative to lipoproteins compared to SEC.
source: We found that, although lipoproteins were still present, DMC and TMC led to a higher purity of EVs relative to lipoproteins (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fractions 9–12 were collected for DMC and TMC to account for the extra 2 ml of resin in the column.
source: We collected fractions 9–12 (instead of fractions 7–10 as for SEC) for DMC and TMC to account for the extra 2 ml of resin in the column (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: DMC and TMC columns significantly depleted ApoB-100 compared to SEC columns.
source: We found that DMC and TMC columns significantly depleted ApoB-100, but also led to some loss in EV yield, particularly CD9, compared to SEC columns (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DMC and TMC columns led to some loss in EV yield, particularly CD9, compared to SEC columns.
source: We found that DMC and TMC columns significantly depleted ApoB-100, but also led to some loss in EV yield, particularly CD9, compared to SEC columns (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DMC and TMC columns had a lower EV yield than SEC.
source: Calculating the relative yields of each tetraspanin and averaging the three tetraspanin ratios to calculate EV yield, we found that DMC and TMC columns had a lower EV yield than SEC but significantly higher EV/ApoB-100 ratios.
evidence: This finding is based on calculations from the Simoa measurements.

claim: DMC and TMC columns had significantly higher EV/ApoB-100 ratios than SEC.
source: Calculating the relative yields of each tetraspanin and averaging the three tetraspanin ratios to calculate EV yield, we found that DMC and TMC columns had a lower EV yield than SEC but significantly higher EV/ApoB-100 ratios.
evidence: This finding is based on calculations from the Simoa measurements.

claim: DMC columns had higher ratios of EVs to ApoB-100 compared to SEC, but the ratio of EVs to albumin remained the same.
source: Although DMC columns had higher ratios of EVs to ApoB-100 compared to SEC, the ratio of EVs to albumin remained the same.
evidence: This finding is based on calculations from the Simoa measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: TMC columns had a higher ratio of both EVs to ApoB-100 and EVs to albumin compared to SEC columns.
source: The TMC column, on the other hand, had a higher ratio of both EVs to ApoB-100 and EVs to albumin compared to the SEC column (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Mass spectrometry-based proteomic analysis was performed to assess the utility of highly pure EVs isolated with TMC.
source: To assess the utility of highly pure EVs isolated with TMC, we performed mass spectrometry-based proteomic analysis.
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure.

claim: Performing mass spectrometry on EVs from plasma is challenging because levels of both free proteins and lipoproteins are several orders of magnitude higher than those of EV proteins.
source: Performing mass spectrometry on EVs from plasma is challenging because levels of both free proteins and lipoproteins are several orders of magnitude higher than those of EV proteins (Smolarz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smolarz et al., 2019.

claim: Using TMC, 780 proteins were detected from EVs isolated from only 1 ml of plasma.
source: Using TMC, we were able to detect 780 proteins from EVs isolated from only 1 ml of plasma (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The results demonstrate the advantage of using TMC for deep proteomics analysis using a small sample volume.
source: These results demonstrate the advantage of using TMC for deep proteomics analysis using a small sample volume.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the proteomics results.

claim: Single-use chromatography columns represent an attractive platform for isolating EVs from clinical samples as they are inexpensive and take a short time to run.
source: Single-use chromatography columns, whether SEC to maximize EV yield or TMC to maximize EV purity, represent an attractive platform for isolating EVs from clinical samples as they are inexpensive and take a short time to run (Monguió-Tortajada et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Monguió-Tortajada et al., 2019.

claim: The throughput of columns is limited.
source: The throughput of columns, however, is limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of column-based methods.

claim: Columns are usually run one at a time.
source: Columns are usually run one at a time, and although it is possible to run more than one column at the same time, this becomes challenging if done manually.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of manual column operation.

claim: Running more than one column at the same time becomes challenging if done manually.
source: Columns are usually run one at a time, and although it is possible to run more than one column at the same time, this becomes challenging if done manually.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of manual column operation.

claim: A semi-automated stand for running eight columns in parallel was built to increase the throughput and reproducibility of column-based EV isolation.
source: To increase the throughput and reproducibility of column-based EV isolation, we built a semi-automated stand for running eight columns in parallel.
evidence: This describes the development of a device shown in Figure 5.

claim: A syringe pump run by a Raspberry Pi was used to dispense liquid to all columns in parallel.
source: Using a syringe pump run by a Raspberry Pi, we were able to dispense liquid to all columns in parallel (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This describes the device shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: High concordance was found between eight SEC columns run by the device and eight SEC columns run manually for EV isolation from plasma.
source: We tested the reproducibility of our device using Simoa and found high concordance between eight SEC columns run by the device and eight SEC columns run manually for EV isolation from plasma (Figure 5C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The device was built as a proof of principle to run eight columns in parallel.
source: Although this device was built as a proof of principle to run eight columns in parallel, we envision building a similar device that could run many more columns simultaneously in the future.
evidence: This is a statement about the purpose and limitations of the current device.

claim: A similar device that could run many more columns simultaneously is envisioned for the future.
source: Although this device was built as a proof of principle to run eight columns in parallel, we envision building a similar device that could run many more columns simultaneously in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future developments.

claim: Methods to enrich EVs from both lipoproteins and free proteins in plasma were developed based on the ability to measure proteins associated with these different components using ultrasensitive assays.
source: In this work, we developed methods to enrich EVs from both lipoproteins and free proteins in plasma based on our ability to measure proteins associated with these different components using ultrasensitive assays.
evidence: This summarizes the main contribution of the work.

claim: The ApoB-100 assay was combined with previously developed Simoa assays for the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81, as well as albumin.
source: We then combined this assay with previously developed Simoa assays for the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81, as well as albumin (Ter-Ovanesyan et al., 2021; Norman et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the combination of assays used in the study.

claim: With the combined assays, EVs, free proteins, and lipoproteins from the same sample could be quantified on one experimental platform.
source: With these assays in place, we were able to quantify EVs, free proteins, and lipoproteins from the same sample on one experimental platform.
evidence: This describes the capability enabled by the combined assays.

claim: Different ways of separating EVs from lipoproteins were assessed with the aim of developing improved EV isolation methods.
source: Using this approach, we assessed different ways of separating EVs from lipoproteins with the aim of developing improved EV isolation methods.
evidence: This describes the overall approach of the study.

claim: Plasma contains several types of lipoproteins with varying protein and lipid compositions.
source: Plasma contains several types of lipoproteins with varying protein and lipid compositions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about plasma lipoproteins.

claim: There is not a single protein present on all lipoproteins.
source: Although there is not a single present on all lipoproteins, we chose to measure ApoB-100, as it is a protein component of several lipoproteins (such as LDL, IDL, and VLDL) that overlap in size with EVs (Simonsen, 2017; Johnsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about lipoprotein composition.

claim: ApoB-100 was chosen as a marker because it is a protein component of several lipoproteins (such as LDL, IDL, and VLDL) that overlap in size with EVs.
source: Although there is not a single present on all lipoproteins, we chose to measure ApoB-100, as it is a protein component of several lipoproteins (such as LDL, IDL, and VLDL) that overlap in size with EVs (Simonsen, 2017; Johnsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing ApoB-100 as a marker, supported by citations.

claim: The tetraspanin and albumin Simoa assays were previously used to directly compare EV yield and free protein contamination for different SEC resins.
source: We previously used our tetraspanin and albumin Simoa assays to directly compare EV yield and free protein contamination for different SEC resins (Ter-Ovanesyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement cites previous work by the authors.

claim: A similar approach was used to compare EV yield and lipoprotein contamination by including the ApoB-100 assay.
source: Here, we used a similar approach to compare EV yield and lipoprotein contamination by including the ApoB-100 assay and found that we were unable to effectively separate tetraspanins from ApoB-100 by SEC.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Tetraspanins could not be effectively separated from ApoB-100 by SEC.
source: Here, we used a similar approach to compare EV yield and lipoprotein contamination by including the ApoB-100 assay and found that we were unable to effectively separate tetraspanins from ApoB-100 by SEC.
evidence: This finding is based on the SEC experiments with different resins.

claim: Simoa assays were used to evaluate DGC and showed that this technique enables good separation of tetraspanins from ApoB-100 and albumin.
source: We also used our Simoa assays to evaluate DGC and showed that this technique enables good separation of tetraspanins from ApoB-100 and albumin; however, since DGC requires an ultracentrifuge, is low throughput, and time-intensive, it is not suitable for clinical samples.

claim: DGC requires an ultracentrifuge, is low throughput, and time-intensive, and is therefore not suitable for clinical samples.
